Article Title: Trump signs Russia sanctions bill: What it means and will India actually face 100% tariff
Article Text:
The Senate passed the bill 86-11 on August 7. (Photo: ANI)

What does the Russia sanctions law do?

India's Russian oil purchase

Russia Sanctions Bill: What It Means For India

What has India said?

What could a 100% tariff mean for India?

Will India actually face a 100% tariff?

What has China said

US President Donald Trump on Friday signed into law the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration expanded powers to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia and countries that continue significant purchases of Russian oil and gas.The White House said the law expands statutory sanctions, tariffs and prohibitions targeting Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran for five years.The legislation is significant for India because New Delhi remains one of the world's biggest buyers of Russian crude. However, the law does not automatically impose a 100% tariff on Indian goods. Instead, it creates a legal pathway for the Trump administration to impose such tariffs under specified conditions.The legislation targets Russian officials, financial institutions, defence-related networks and the country's so-called “shadow fleet” of vessels used to transport energy while circumventing Western restrictions.A key provision gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest importers of Russian petroleum or natural gas, subject to conditions laid down in the law.It also includes provisions targeting countries that facilitate Russian oil sanctions evasion and extends the Iran Sanctions Act for another five years.The Senate passed the bill 86-11 on August 7, while the House of Representatives approved it 262-159 on Wednesday, sending it to Trump for his signature. The law was named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a leading supporter of the legislation.India's crude sourcing pattern has changed sharply since 2022. Before the Ukraine war, Gulf countries accounted for more than 55% of India's crude supplies, while Russia's share was below 15%, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).Since then, India's purchases from Russia have increased substantially, while the Gulf's share has fallen below 30%.The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that between December 2022 and August 2026, China accounted for around half of Russia's crude exports, followed by India at 37%, Turkey at 5% and the European Union at 5%.Indian refiners have also secured supplies from the US, Brazil, Canada, Venezuela and African producers, but Russian crude remains a major part of India's import basket.India has repeatedly defended its Russian oil purchases, saying its energy policy is driven by the need to secure affordable and reliable supplies for its population.New Delhi said it was "monitoring further developments on this matter" and remained "firmly committed to ensuring energy security" for its people."This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side," the external affairs ministry said.The ministry also said India was determined to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.Indian ambassador to the US Vinay Kwatra said: "India imports over 85% of its crude oil and around half its natural gas. Our sourcing reflects a fundamental national responsibility: looking outside our borders to secure adequate, affordable and uninterrupted energy for our people.""India is the world’s fastest-growing major economy and its third-largest energy consumer. Yet the average Indian consumes less than one-third of the global average and one-tenth of an average American. Our energy needs will, and must, grow,” Kwatra added.New Delhi has repeatedly argued that its purchases of Russian oil are driven by energy security and commercial considerations.“India should not allow US tariff threats to determine its energy policy,” GTRI said, adding that India should continue buying Russian oil as long as it remained commercially competitive and negotiate with Washington without granting unilateral trade concessions.Ajay Srivastava, founder of GTRI and a former trade ministry official, said the legislation was a pressure tactic against India.“The bill is a blunt and dangerous attempt to pressurise India to sign the bilateral trade agreement on one-sided terms. India buys Russian oil to secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people, not to finance war, and these purchases have helped stabilise global supplies and prices,” he said, according to BBC.“Tariffs of up to 100% would punish Indian exporters and American consumers, disrupt trade and give the US president excessive power over major partners," he added.If the US eventually imposes steep tariffs on Indian goods under the new law, the biggest impact would be on Indian exports to the US rather than directly on the price of Russian crude.A tariff of up to 100% could make Indian products substantially more expensive in the American market and affect exporters across sectors.Higher import duties could reduce the competitiveness of Indian goods, although the actual impact would depend on the rate imposed, the products covered and how Washington implements the measure.The legislation therefore adds another layer of uncertainty to India-US trade ties, at a time when Washington and New Delhi are already negotiating a broader trade agreement, while India's dependence on Russian crude remains substantial.Not immediately. The law gives Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that meet specified criteria, but it does not itself impose a 100% tariff on India or China.India is particularly exposed because it remains one of the world's biggest buyers of Russian crude, while China is the largest buyer of Russian oil.The legislation also gives the president waiver authority under specified conditions, including certification to Congress that a waiver is in the national interest.This means the impact on India will depend on whether and how the Trump administration uses the new powers, as well as the eventual tariff rate, products covered and implementation timeline.The legislation is intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow by reducing the revenues Russia earns from energy exports. Supporters of the measure have argued that sanctions and tariffs can increase pressure on Russia and push it towards ending the war in Ukraine.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the legislation, describing sanctions as an important tool to pressure Russia towards peace.Russia, however, criticised the move. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was monitoring the legislation and described additional US sanctions as “unfriendly actions”.“We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the US would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine,” Peskov told reporters, according to Reuters.China has also rejected the US use of tariffs against countries buying Russian energy. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing opposed US “long-arm jurisdiction”.“China consistently opposes long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law and is not authorised by the United Nations Security Council,” Guo said.“China has always conducted normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” he said. “Such cooperation neither targets any third party nor is subject to interference or coercion from any third party,” Guo added.China buys more Russian crude than India, but much of its Russian energy imports are transported through pipelines across the two countries' land border.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday signed into law the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation is significant for India because New Delhi remains one of the world's biggest buyers of Russian crude. The law does not automatically impose a 100% tariff on Indian goods. Instead, it creates a legal pathway for the Trump administration to impose such tariffs under specified conditions.

Article Title: ‘Treated on floor, verandah’: Dhaka hospitals struggle to find space for dengue patients
Article Text:
Patients infected with dengue receive treatment at a hospital in Dhaka

Patients treated on floors, verandas

Dengue spreads beyond Dhaka

October could bring further rise

A sharp rise in dengue cases is putting hospitals in Dhaka under severe pressure. Over 747 new patients were admitted across Bangladesh in the 24 hours to 8am on Friday. The surge prompted some hospitals to treat patients on floors and verandas after beds filled up.According to a report by Dhaka Tribune, at Mugda General Hospital in Dhaka, 145 dengue patients were receiving treatment in a ward with a capacity of just 38 beds on Thursday. Doctors and nurses said the overcrowding was making it harder to monitor patients, administer medicines and provide emergency care.The directorate general of health services (DGHS) said no dengue deaths were reported during the latest 24-hour period. However, 79 dengue deaths have been recorded in the first 18 days of September alone.Since January 1, 59,147 people have been hospitalised with dengue across Bangladesh, with 176 deaths reported. A total of 54,838 patients have been discharged after treatment.At Mugda General Hospital, every designated bed in the dengue ward was occupied. Additional patients were being treated on the floor and veranda, while some beds were being shared by more than one patient.Afrin Akter, from Narayanganj, was among those being treated on the floor. She was vomiting intermittently and appeared too weak to speak properly as a nurse administered saline.Her mother said Afrin had suffered from fever and body aches for several days. After medicines failed to improve her condition, the family tried to get her admitted to several hospitals but could not find a vacant bed.They eventually reached Mugda General Hospital, where Afrin was admitted despite the lack of a bed.Nasima, sub-in-charge of the hospital, said patients were arriving every day from Dhaka and districts outside the capital.“Due to the bed shortage, patients are being admitted to the floor and veranda out of necessity,” she said.She said 145 patients were currently being treated in the ward against its capacity of 38 beds. Many patients, she added, arrive in critical condition, while early treatment can improve the chances of recovery.Dr Nurul Islam, deputy director of Mugda General Hospital, said the increase in dengue cases had pushed up patient pressure.“At present, services are being continued with the existing doctors and nurses, but additional beds and manpower are needed to handle the situation,” he said.“All the patients who are coming here are being admitted and provided treatment. Instructions have been given to every ward to provide proper treatment.”The latest DGHS figures show that the pressure is not limited to the capital.Of the 747 patients admitted nationwide in the latest 24-hour period, 216 were admitted outside Dhaka's city corporations but within Dhaka division. Another 61 were admitted in Dhaka North City and 40 in Dhaka South.Chittagong division recorded 180 admissions, while 92 patients were admitted in Mymensingh, 81 in Khulna, 52 in Rangpur and 25 in Barisal.August was the worst month for dengue this year, with 20,536 infections and 43 deaths reported.Entomologist professor Kabirul Bashar said forecast models indicate that the dengue situation could worsen further in October.Although Aedes mosquitoes become less visible as winter approaches, he said they should not be neglected.Referring to Bangladesh as a “country of mosquitoes,” Bashar said dengue cases were rising compared with previous years and warned that the situation could become more severe in the coming days.He called for greater public awareness about Aedes mosquito behaviour and stronger mosquito-control measures.DGHS director general professor Dr Prabhat Chandra Biswas said patients would be referred to private hospitals if government facilities exceeded their capacity.He said hospitals had been instructed to increase their bed capacity and that treatment facilities were also being strengthened at district and upazila levels in dengue-prone areas.Public health expert Dr Mushtak Hossain said treating patients alone would not be enough to control the outbreak.“The long-term effective solution is to destroy the breeding grounds of Aedes mosquitoes,” he said.He called for regular mosquito control, greater public awareness and early detection and treatment at the local level, along with adequate facilities in Dhaka and across districts and upazilas.
Article Summary: Over 747 new patients were admitted across Bangladesh in the 24 hours to 8am on Friday. At Mugda General Hospital in Dhaka, 145 dengue patients were receiving treatment in a ward with a capacity of 38 beds. Doctors and nurses said the overcrowding was making it harder to monitor patients, administer medicines and provide emergency care.

Article Title: World's last known wild Chilean tree daisy gets a lifeline as conservationists use ropes to support its only survivor and two seedlings arrive at a Scottish garden
Article Text:
Image: Wikimedia

World's rarest wild Chilean tree daisy clings to life

Scientists collect 29 seeds from the last known wild tree

Image: BBC

Two seedlings arrive at Logan Botanic Garden in Scotland

International conservationists work against extinction

Why scientists are growing the seedlings outside Chile

Conservation efforts offer hope for the species

A rare tree daisy from Chile's Robinson Crusoe Island is receiving a new lifeline after two seedlings arrived at Logan Botanic Garden in south-west Scotland. Dendroseris neriifolia has been reduced to one known wild tree, which grows on a steep cliff and is supported by ropes to prevent it from falling. Conservationists in Chile and the UK are working to preserve the species through seed collection and cultivation. In May 2026, 29 seeds were collected from the surviving tree and sent to Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Eight seedlings germinated, and two have since been transferred to Logan, where specialists hope to learn more about their growth and help secure the future of the critically endangered plant.The remaining wild Dendroseris neriifolia tree grows on a steep volcanic outcrop on Robinson Crusoe Island. Its precarious position has made physical support essential, with ropes helping prevent the tree from falling. The species has experienced a sharp decline over several decades. By 1980, only eight wild trees remained. Reintroduction projects were attempted in the early 2000s, but the breakdown of protective measures in 2017 allowed invasive plants and grazing animals to threaten the site again.The Chilean tree daisy has been affected by widespread forest clearance, intensive grazing by introduced mammals, invasive vegetation and repeated fires.These pressures have damaged the natural habitat on which the species depends. Robinson Crusoe Island is part of the Juan Fernández Archipelago, a group of islands recognised for its distinctive native flora. The restricted distribution of Dendroseris neriifolia makes the loss of its remaining wild population particularly significant.In May 2026, conservationists collected 29 seeds from the surviving tree and sent them to the Millennium Seed Bank at Kew Wakehurst in England. Kew's analysis found that 25 seeds were potentially viable. Eight seedlings subsequently germinated. The work provides an opportunity to preserve plant material from the wild survivor and investigate cultivation methods for the species. The seed collection is part of a broader conservation effort that includes previous collections and restoration projects intended to support the recovery of the tree daisy on its native island.Two of the germinated seedlings have now been transferred to Logan Botanic Garden in Dumfries and Galloway. The remaining germinated plants will stay at Kew and Logan is known for its mild climate, which allows it to cultivate plants from warmer regions. Its experience with species from the Juan Fernández Islands makes it a suitable location for growing the young tree daisies. Richard Baines, curator at Logan, said the arrival of the seedlings was a significant moment for everyone involved. He explained that the garden would provide a safe place for the plants while specialists learn more about their development and adaptation to different environments.The project involves conservationists and scientists from Chile and the UK. Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, Chile's National Forest Corporation and the Juan Fernández National Park are among the organisations involved in the conservation effort. Diego Penneckamp, a scientist at Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, described the work as a race against time. He said the international collaboration could help prevent the extinction of a species with a unique evolutionary history. Felipe Saez, a plant biotechnology engineer and administrator of Parque Nacional Archipiélago Juan Fernández, also highlighted the significance of the seed transfer for protecting the archipelago's native plant life.The seedlings at Logan and Kew provide a form of ex-situ conservation, which involves protecting species outside their natural habitats. This approach can help safeguard plants when wild populations face severe threats.Growing the seedlings to maturity could allow researchers to study their development and potentially produce additional seeds. However, the long-term success of the programme will depend on the plants' ability to survive, reproduce and contribute to future conservation work.The wider Dendroseris genus is endemic to the Juan Fernández Islands. Kew has also identified conservation concerns affecting other species within the genus, underscoring the importance of protecting the archipelago's unique biodiversity.The arrival of two seedlings at Logan Botanic Garden marks a new stage in the effort to preserve Dendroseris neriifolia. The wild tree remains on Robinson Crusoe Island, where ropes are helping protect it from falling, while its offspring are being cultivated in the UK.The project combines field conservation in Chile with seed banking and horticultural expertise in Britain. By maintaining plants outside the wild, conservationists hope to develop a stronger foundation for protecting the species and supporting its future recovery.
Article Summary: Dendroseris neriifolia has been reduced to one known wild tree. Conservationists in Chile and the UK are working to preserve the species. In May 2026, 29 seeds were collected from the surviving tree and sent to Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Eight seedlings germinated, and two have since been transferred to Logan Botanic Garden in south-west Scotland.

Article Title: After Jantar Mantar setback, AIMPLB plans 3-month national UCC campaign, to take battle to states
Article Text:
(File photo) The All India Muslim Personal Law Board





NEW DELHI: The All India Muslim Personal Law Board ( AIMPLB ) on Thursday postponed its proposed dharna against the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) at Jantar Mantar after Delhi Police denied permission, citing the "likelihood of a large gathering and difficulty in managing the crowd".The Board said it had assured authorities that the demonstration would be peaceful and described assembly and protest as constitutional rights. AIMPLB spokesperson S Q R Ilyas, however, advised supporters planning to travel to Delhi not to proceed, asking them to avoid inconvenience and maintain peace.The demonstration was planned to mark the Delhi launch of the Board's three-month 'Save India, Save Sharia' campaign, also described as its 'Movement for Protection of Constitution and Sharia', to mobilise public opinion on constitutional rights, religious freedom and Muslim personal law.At an "emergency" press conference, president Maulana Khalid Saifullah Rahmani, spokesperson Dr Syed Qasim Rasool Ilyas and general secretary Maulana Mohd Fazlur Rahim Mujaddidi criticised the denial and said the campaign would continue through other democratic and legal means. The Board plans to hold public-awareness programmes and legal conventions in Hyderabad, Mumbai, Kolkata and Bengaluru, besides reaching out to religious leaders of other faiths, civil rights groups and tribal communities.The Board has already taken its opposition to the UCC and Waqf law to court. After Uttarakhand notified its UCC on January 27, 2025, AIMPLB filed a challenge in the Uttarakhand High Court in February. After the Gujarat Assembly passed its UCC Bill in March 2026, the Board announced in April that it would challenge the legislation in the Gujarat High Court.Separately, AIMPLB moved the Supreme Court against the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, filing its petition in April 2025. The plea challenges the amendments on constitutional grounds, including Articles 14, 25 and 26 — the Right to Equality, Freedom of Religion (Individual), and Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs (Group).The Board also announced a comprehensive 'White Paper' documenting what it describes as "discrimination against minorities and violations of constitutional and religious freedoms", besides setting out its legal objections to the Waqf law. Its proposed charter will cover the UCC, religious freedom, protection of waqf properties and religious places, hate crimes, alleged unlawful demolitions and equal enforcement of law. It is to be submitted to President Droupadi Murmu, seeking protection of minority rights under Articles 25 to 30.The police decision came amid renewed scrutiny of restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar. On Thursday, the Delhi High Court questioned the police over its refusal to allow another proposed protest at the venue and asked how a blanket ban on demonstrations could be justified. Article Title: From daily-wage labourer to entrepreneur: How Aajeevika Mission changed Sonbhadra woman’s life
Article Text:
Nirmala's journey in Sonbhadra showcases Aajeevika Mission's impact on rural women (AI image)

How

Aajeevika Mission

Transformed Nirmala’s Life in Sonbhadra

Aajeevika Mission: From women’s groups to

economic empowerment

Diversification creates a stronger livelihood

One woman’s success inspires an entire village

From self-reliance to market expansion

A model of women-led

rural development





In the tribal and economically backward regions of Uttar Pradesh, a quiet transformation is taking place. Women who were once dependent on agricultural work and daily-wage labour for household survival are increasingly becoming entrepreneurs, managing businesses and contributing significantly to their families’ incomes.The story of Nirmala, a Scheduled Caste woman from Bichpai village in Robertsganj block of Sonbhadra district, is a compelling example of this change. Once dependent on daily wages, Nirmala of Bichpai village in Sonbhadra now earns around Rs 2.5 lakh annually. Her journey from labourer to entrepreneur reflects how the Aajeevika Mission is creating new opportunities for women in Uttar Pradesh’s rural and backward regions.Once compelled to work as a daily-wage labourer to support her six-member family, Nirmala has today established a diversified rural enterprise. Her annual income has risen to approximately Rs 2.5 lakh, while her success has inspired nearly 12 to 15 other women in her village to explore livelihood opportunities and move towards self-reliance.At the heart of this transformation is the Aajeevika Mission, being implemented by the Uttar Pradesh government to organize rural women into Self-Help Groups (SHGs), build their skills, facilitate access to financial assistance and encourage them to establish sustainable livelihood activities.The basic idea behind the Aajeevika Mission is to ensure that rural women are not merely recipients of welfare but become active participants in the rural economy.Through Self-Help Groups, women are brought together and encouraged to develop savings habits, acquire livelihood skills, access financial support and undertake income-generating activities. The SHG platform provides women with a collective support system that can help them overcome one of the biggest barriers faced by poor rural households—the lack of capital and access to organized livelihood opportunities. Nirmala’s journey demonstrates how this approach can translate into tangible economic empowerment.A graduate, Nirmala had the educational qualifications to aspire for a better future, but her family’s weak economic condition limited her opportunities. Her family consisted of her husband, three daughters and a son. Despite managing household responsibilities, she was forced to undertake wage labour to supplement the family income.Joining a Self-Help Group under the Aajeevika Mission became the first major turning point in her life. Instead of remaining dependent on irregular wage employment, Nirmala was introduced to skill development and livelihood opportunities. She received training in candle-making, a relatively low-investment activity with strong seasonal demand, particularly during festivals.She decided to convert this newly acquired skill into an enterprise. Seed capital turned s a skill into a business. Training alone cannot create a successful enterprise unless women also have access to the resources required to put their skills into practice. This is where financial assistance under the livelihood-development ecosystem became crucial for Nirmala.Recognizing her initiative, the Udyamita Vikas Pariyojana provided her with Rs 60,000 in seed money as initial assistance. For Nirmala, this support became the starting capital for her enterprise. She used the money to purchase moulds for making candles in different designs and shapes. Rather than limiting herself to conventional candles, she began producing attractive, colourful designer candles in the form of flowers, trees and other decorative figures.Initially, she focused on the festival market, particularly Deepawali, when demand for decorative candles rises sharply. What began as a seasonal activity gradually developed into a regular business as customers responded positively to her products. The transformation is significant: the woman who once sold her labour for daily wages was now producing a marketable product of her own.Nirmala’s journey also demonstrates another important principle of the Aajeevika Mission—livelihood diversification. Instead of depending on a single product, she gradually expanded her enterprise into different activities. With support from the Khadi Gramodyog Department, she received a popcorn-making machine, adding another source of income.She subsequently received specialized training from the Food Safety and Food Processing Department. The two-month training programme equipped her with skills to prepare value-added food products such as rose gulkand, sharbat and gajar ka murabba (carrot preserve).Nirmala now produces these products according to seasonal demand. This diversification has helped her move beyond a single festival-dependent enterprise towards a broader rural business model. Designer candles provide opportunities during the festive season, while food-processing products create additional avenues for income during other periods.In this way, different government interventions have complemented one another—SHG mobilization, skill development, seed capital, equipment support and food-processing training—to help convert a rural woman’s potential into a sustainable livelihood.Household responsibilities no longer stand in the wayNirmala’s success also challenges the traditional perception that women in rural areas can engage in economic activity only when they are relieved of household responsibilities. She continues to manage her family while simultaneously running her enterprise.This is one of the important social outcomes of the Aajeevika Mission. When livelihood activities are designed around the circumstances of rural women and are supported with training, finance and local opportunities, women can combine entrepreneurship with their responsibilities at home.The result is not merely an increase in income. It brings greater confidence, decision-making ability and social recognition. For Nirmala, entrepreneurship has given her an identity beyond that of a wage labourer.The most powerful impact of Nirmala’s story can perhaps be seen in the women around her. Her success has encouraged 12 to 15 women in the village to move towards self-reliance. Her journey has demonstrated that entrepreneurship is possible even in a rural and economically disadvantaged area, provided women receive the right combination of training, institutional support and access to capital.This is precisely the larger objective of the Aajeevika Mission: creating an ecosystem in which one empowered woman can become a catalyst for change within her community. The transformation therefore extends beyond individual income. As more women join SHGs and take up enterprises, the economic role of women within rural households and communities becomes stronger.Nirmala is not stopping at her current achievements. Her next objective is to take her products to the online marketplace. This aspiration reflects the changing character of rural entrepreneurship in Uttar Pradesh.The journey that began with selling candles locally is now moving towards wider markets. Digital platforms can potentially help rural entrepreneurs overcome geographical limitations and connect their products with customers beyond their villages and districts. Nirmala’s ambition to enter the online market is therefore another important step—from local production to market expansion.Nirmala’s story illustrates the potential of a well-connected rural livelihood ecosystem.The Aajeevika Mission provided the institutional foundation by bringing her into the Self-Help Group network. Skill training gave her the capability to produce marketable goods. Seed money enabled her to purchase the equipment and raw materials necessary to begin production. Departmental support helped diversify her enterprise, while further training opened the door to food processing.The result is a woman who has moved from wage labour to entrepreneurship, from economic dependence to self-reliance and from individual struggle to becoming an inspiration for other women. Her journey also reflects the broader vision of the Yogi government to strengthen rural economies by empowering women as economic actors. In backward and tribal regions, where conventional employment opportunities can be limited, women-led micro-enterprises can provide an important alternative source of household income.Nirmala’s colourful candles may have been the first product of her enterprise, but they have come to symbolize something much larger—a new confidence among rural women. Today, Nirmala earns around Rs 2.5 lakh a year, manages her household and runs a diversified enterprise. More importantly, her story is encouraging other women in Bichpai to believe that self-reliance is possible.From a daily-wage worker to a rural entrepreneur, Nirmala’s journey is a powerful example of how Aajeevika Mission can transform skills into livelihoods, livelihoods into enterprises and individual success into a movement for women-led rural development.(District Transformation)
Article Summary: Aajeevika Mission is creating new opportunities for women in Uttar Pradesh’s rural and backward regions. Nirmala of Bichpai village in Sonbhadra now earns around Rs 2.5 lakh annually. Her success has inspired nearly 12 to 15 other women in her village to explore livelihood opportunities.

Elon Musk wants AI companies to test each other’s models

“grading your own homework

xAI and SpaceX are expanding their AI operations

Elon Musk has a message for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about rival Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) companies. Instead of complaining, the world’s richest person has advised Altman, Amodei, and other leading AI companies to work with Chinese AI firms. Musk has recommended that both American and Chinese AI companies independently test each other’s models before releasing them to the public.Speaking at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Musk proposed that companies including xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and three or four leading Chinese AI companies allow rivals to run a common “test harness” on their models. His proposal comes as AI leaders debate how quickly the technology should be developed and how governments should regulate it, while concerns about Chinese models and competition with China continue to grow.Musk said AI companies should stop” and instead allow competitors to examine their models for potential safety concerns before public release.Musk explained.Under the proposal, leading AI companies would use a common testing system to evaluate one another’s models.Musk acknowledged that the approach may not be perfect, but argued that involving competitors would increase the chances of identifying potential problems.Musk said.Musk said the approach should involve Chinese AI companies as well, rather than limiting the process to US-based AI labs. He added that the proposal could be implemented quickly and suggested that China may be willing to participate.Musk said.Musk's comments come after a weekend of heightened discussion around AI safety involving some of the industry's most prominent executives. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman were among the technology leaders who backed a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down AI development.The discussion intensified after Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at Anthropic and OpenAI, announced that he had left Anthropic and argued that leading AI labs were taking significant risks with the technology. Evan Hubinger, an alignment lead at Anthropic, backed Coxon's comments.Hubinger wrote.Amodei has separately suggested that AI companies could use third-party technology assessments involving “embedded evaluators” to verify whether companies are following appropriate safety practices.The discussion around slowing AI development has also become linked to competition between the US and China. US President Donald Trump has argued that imposing limits on AI development could allow China to gain an advantage in the technology.Amodei has also described balancing AI safety with competition against China as the “toughest dilemma.”Meanwhile, China's Foreign Ministry criticised calls to slow AI development. A spokesperson described the AI industry's push asaccording to a Reuters translation of the remarks.Musk's proposal would bring Chinese AI companies into the model-testing process rather than treating the country's AI industry solely as a competitor. He suggested that having companies from both sides test one another's systems could provide another layer of scrutiny.The US administration has pushed back against calls from technology leaders for greater restrictions on AI development. Trump described concerns around AI as a “hoax” and a “scam” in posts on Truth Social.National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett also said the private sector was the “right place” to address concerns around AI, while adding that the government would continue monitoring the industry and use law enforcement when necessary.Musk's own companies have also challenged some state-level AI regulations. xAI has sued California over its AI Training Data Transparency Act, also known as AB 2013, and sued Minnesota over legislation targeting so-called nudify applications.At the same time, SpaceX's AI business has faced probes and lawsuits after Grok's image-generation capabilities were used to create and distribute non-consensual sexualised deepfake images, including material involving minors.Musk's comments come as his companies continue to expand their presence in AI. SpaceX acquired xAI in February, bringing Musk's AI business under the SpaceX umbrella. The combined company is working on Grok models and AI tools aimed at competing with products from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.The company also completed an acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor for $60 billion in August, according to the report.Against this backdrop, Musk's proposal would place rival AI companies, including Chinese firms, in a shared model-testing framework. He said the companies have not yet agreed to the idea, but argued that it could be a practical step toward identifying safety issues before AI models reach the public.
Article Summary: Elon Musk wants AI companies to test each other’s models. Suggests Chinese AI companies be included in the testing process. Article Title: Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke to employees: Don't make AI do all your work, it does not add value only ...
Article Text:
Image courtesy: LinkedIn

Duolingo's CEO tells a similar story

The rise of 'workslop'

The cost is climbing

Shopify cofounder and CEO Tobias Lütke has shifted his stance on workplace AI use, cautioning employees not to let the technology do all their work. According to a report by Fortune, speaking on The Knowledge Project podcast, Lütke said staff were producing unexamined emails and code with AI, creating what he called “slop grenades” that burden colleagues with cleanup. “You’re just letting AI do the work for you,” he warned, noting that AI should synthesize points in an email rather than generate long, sloppy missives.Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low-value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslop, while 38% reported receiving it. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.Lütke isn't alone in reversing course. Duolingo CEO Luis von Ahn made headlines last year for declaring the company would go "AI-first" — a policy that tied employee evaluations to AI usage, replaced human contractors with AI tools, and limited headcount growth to only what automation couldn't handle.By May, though, Von Ahn was telling Fast Company he'd been swept up by how convincing AI-generated writing looked in demos, without accounting for how it holds up at scale compared to human creativity. He pointed to Duolingo's need to produce large volumes of story content for language lessons, estimating a meaningful share of AI-scaled output ends up being low-quality filler that has to be caught before it reaches users.Researchers now have a name for exactly what Lütke and Von Ahn are describing: workslop — AI-generated output that looks polished and complete on the surface but lacks the substance to actually be useful, forcing someone else to redo the work.A survey of 962 full-time American desk workers conducted this year by BetterUp Labs and Stanford's Social Media Lab found that more than half of respondents (52.7%) admitted to sending workslop to a colleague, a habit that showed up more often in workplaces that actively encouraged AI adoption. More than a third (38%) said they had been on the receiving end of it, spending an average of 3.4 hours a month cleaning it up. Common examples cited included emails with broken links or code that was needlessly overcomplicated.The damage isn't just measured in wasted hours. The survey found that workslop erodes trust between coworkers — recipients rated colleagues who sent it as less competent and less friendly, and more than a third of those who'd received it said they'd actively try to avoid working with that person again in the future.This year's findings mark a worsening trend compared to last year's version of the same survey, when 40% of respondents reported encountering workslop and said cleanup took roughly two hours on average. That earlier figure translated to about $186 in lost productivity per affected employee each month, or as much as $9 million annually in lost productivity for a 10,000-person organization — a number that's now almost certainly higher given this year's longer average cleanup time.
Article Summary: Researchers have coined the term workslop to describe polished-looking but low- value AI output that drags down productivity. A survey by BetterUp Labs and Stanford’s Social Media Lab found that over half of U.S. desk workers admitted to sending workslops. On average, employees spent 3.4 hours per month revising AI-generated work, costing organizations millions in lost productivity.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just told OpenAI, your view of AI as 'new form of Alien mind' is wrong, it is just ...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

‘It’s just engineering’ says Jensen Huang

The essay that started it

Two very different worldviews

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back against OpenAI ’s recent description of artificial intelligence as a “new form of alien mind,” arguing that AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. According to a report by TechCrunch, speaking at a tech conference this week, Huang said, “AI isn’t alien—it’s mathematics, algorithms, and data shaped by human intent. ” His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.Huang emphasised that AI’s evolution should be viewed through the lens of engineering rather than existential speculation. “We’re not building aliens,” he said. “We’re building machines that learn patterns and optimize outcomes. It’s just engineering—nothing mystical.” The Nvidia chief has long argued that AI development should remain grounded in scientific rigor and practical application, not philosophical fear.On that basis, Huang said no new laws or regulations are needed to govern AI, arguing instead that market pressure alone will push companies to avoid releasing unsafe products.Companies, he said, should simply pace themselves and pause development if they lose confidence in a product's safety, rather than waiting for external rules to force that discipline.He also pushed back on the framing that safety and speed are competing priorities, telling attendees that innovation and safe products aren't a "false choice" — companies, in his view, can pursue both at once without regulatory intervention slowing them down. He used the moment to reaffirm his own ambitions for Nvidia's growth too, saying the AI boom has left him more ambitious than ever about the company's and the industry's prospects.Huang's comments were a direct response to Pachocki's essay "An Alien Mind," published on OpenAI's blog earlier this month. In it, Pachocki reflected on the trajectory of reasoning models since 2023 and warned that AI intelligence is grown through massive-scale optimization rather than deliberately designed, resulting in systems whose internal reasoning increasingly escapes full human understanding.He argued that as these systems approach and potentially exceed human capability on many fronts, alignment — ensuring AI reliably acts according to human values, even when unsupervised — remains an unsolved and urgent problem. Pachocki called for stronger technical safeguards, broader international coordination, and industry-wide safety commitments enforceable by third-party auditors or government bodies. He stated plainly that he believes no AI lab has yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to justify scaling at maximum speed for much longer.The exchange highlights a widening philosophical split among AI's most influential figures: hardware and infrastructure leaders like Huang, whose business benefits from AI scaling continuing unimpeded, versus AI lab researchers like Pachocki, who are increasingly vocal that the technology's own developers cannot yet fully explain or control what they're building.Notably, Huang did not directly address recent real-world incidents cited by critics of the "leave it to industry" approach — including an OpenAI model reportedly breaching Hugging Face's systems, and separate lawsuits alleging harm linked to extended chatbot conversations. He also stopped short of proposing a formal industry self-regulation framework, an approach some in the field see as a more plausible middle ground than either strict government regulation or no oversight at all.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says AI is not an otherworldly consciousness but a human-made computational tool. His comments came shortly after OpenAI published a blog post titled “An Alien Mind,” which suggested that advanced AI systems might think in ways fundamentally different from humans.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences

In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.
